Dear Sion Buckler

Thank you for your email.

Your request has been handled in line with data protection legislation as a Subject Access Request (SAR) for your personal information. In order for us to process your request we require further information as detailed below.

Verifying Identity

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) is committed to protecting your personal data and keeping it secure. One of the key safeguards we use is verifying the identity of anyone who requests access to personal data. This ensures that only you can access your information through a SAR.
To process your request, we ask that you provide two forms of identification.

  1.  Photo ID - This should clearly show your face, such as a passport or driving licence.

  1.  Proof of Address - This should show your full name and current address, such as a utility bill (e.g. electricity, gas, water, telephone/broadband), council tax bill, or a bank/credit card statement. These documents must be dated within the last six months.
You can use your driving licence as proof of your current address, but you'll still need to provide an additional photo ID (such as your passport).

We do not use photo ID to confirm your likeness but because the process for obtaining photo ID involves additional safeguards that help us confirm your identity with greater confidence. This is a necessary and proportionate step to make sure your data remains secure.
You can find more information about how we handle personal data in our Personal Information Charter<https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/ministry-of-justice/about/personal-information-charter>

On receipt of this information, we will continue to process your request.

External Email: Take care with attachments & links.

Ordnance Survey Historical Enquiries Team,

I am writing to request information regarding historical Ordnance Survey mapping and naming conventions for a specific area in Llandough, near Penarth, Vale of Glamorgan (Wales).

I am researching the historical depiction of a property and surrounding land historically referred to as Ty Mawr / Great House Farm, and I am trying to understand how its labelling and placement may have changed across Ordnance Survey map editions.

Specific mapping references
The area I am examining includes the following Ordnance Survey historical map references:
38-1-608
38-1-334

I am also comparing Ordnance Survey map editions from approximately the 1950s through to the early 1970s.

Mapping issue being investigated
From comparing available historical map editions, I have observed the following:

Earlier Ordnance Survey maps (pre-1950s / early 1950s) appear to consistently show the name Ty Mawr / Great House Farm in one field or parcel location.

In later editions (circa early 1970s), the label “Ty Mawr” appears to shift position between adjacent parcels, and the descriptor “Farm” appears to be applied or positioned differently than in earlier mapping.

There also appears to be a change in how the surrounding land parcels are labelled or visually grouped.

What I am seeking clarification on
Could you please advise:

Whether Ordnance Survey records show any map revision notes, resurvey information, or internal documentation explaining changes in naming or label placement for this area between approximately 1950 and 1975
Whether changes such as the movement of a name between adjacent parcels would typically result from:

resurvey work or updated field recording
cartographic generalisation or redraw practices
changes in naming conventions or feature classification
Whether OS holds any guidance or archival material explaining how estate names or farm names were assigned, repositioned, or reinterpreted across map editions in this period

Which historical Ordnance Survey editions or map series would best show the most accurate progression of naming and label placement for this specific site

If possible, I would also appreciate guidance on accessing any archived mapping sheets or revision history material relevant to this location.

Thank you for your assistance. I appreciate your time in helping clarify how Ordnance Survey mapping practices evolved during this period.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergenant)
Military Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional
Life Member @ Royal Signals

Sirs/Ma'am,

I am writing regarding historical records for *Great House Farm (Ty Mawr)*
on the north side of Leckwith Road, Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan (title
WA231076 / formerly WA240304 accordingly to Land Registry FOI).

My family (Williams, later Buckler) are believed to have held the land,
with acquisition around *1876*. I have two OS map references for the same

Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman,

I wish to submit a complaint of maladministration concerning the handling
of enforcement and associated administrative processes relating to my
family’s former residence and land at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr),
Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan, culminating in its demolition in December
1988.

This complaint is not a request to reopen any court judgment. It concerns
the *administrative conduct of public bodies*, including notice procedures,
enforcement execution, and heritage-related decision-making.
1. Defective and misleading notice process

I believe that formal notices issued during the relevant period were
materially defective, including being addressed to “Mrs Buckler” rather
than the legal occupier, Mary Williams.

This created a situation where the intended recipient was not properly
identified in their correct legal capacity, which I believe resulted in a *loss
of meaningful opportunity to respond, challenge, or seek suspension of
enforcement action* at the relevant time.
2. Loss of opportunity to contest enforcement

As a result of the above notice issues, I believe the family was deprived
of a genuine opportunity to take timely legal or procedural steps to
prevent or delay enforcement action, including demolition.

This constitutes, in my view, procedural unfairness in the administration
of enforcement.
3. Heritage and regulatory oversight concerns

I also believe that relevant public authorities had knowledge of the
historical and archaeological significance of the site, including Roman and
early medieval features, but failed to take adequate protective action
prior to demolition.

This raises concerns of *regulatory failure in the exercise of statutory
heritage responsibilities*.
4. Irreversible loss and harm

The outcome of these processes was the complete demolition of the property
in December 1988, resulting in:

   - irreversible loss of a long-occupied family home
   - destruction of potential historical and archaeological material
   - loss of personal and family property and records

I believe this outcome resulted from administrative failings rather than a
fair and properly informed process.
------------------------------
5. What I am asking the Ombudsman to do

I am requesting that the Ombudsman:

   1. Investigate whether there was maladministration in:
      - service of notices and identification of the correct legal occupier
      - execution of enforcement actions
      - handling of heritage-related responsibilities by relevant
      authorities
   2. Determine whether these actions caused a loss of opportunity to
   prevent or challenge demolition.
   3. Consider whether a finding of maladministration is appropriate, and
   whether this should lead to:
      - a formal apology
      - a recommendation for ex gratia compensation
      - any further remedial or restorative measures within the Ombudsman’s
      remit

------------------------------
6. Supporting material

I am in the process of obtaining further documentary evidence via Freedom
of Information requests and archival sources, including:

   - enforcement and court execution records
   - local authority and heritage body correspondence
   - any relevant ministerial communications

I will provide these as they become available.
------------------------------

I submit this complaint in good faith and seek an independent review of
administrative fairness and decision-making, not a reopening of any
judicial determination.

Regards, Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sgt)

Dear Mr Buckler,

I have undertaken a reasonable search of our records and would advise 
you as follows:

a) The minutes of all council minutes for the period in question were 
deposited in the Glamorgan Records Office in 2002. These cover the 
period from 1982 when Llandough Community Council was first formed. 
Prior to that time, the community of Llandough was included in the remit 
of Penarth Town Council. The relevant web-link which shows the 
information held is : perihttps://glamarchives.gov.uk/od

b) You are able to visit the Glamorgan Records Office in Cardiff by 
appointment and the web-link to find details of their location is: 
https://glamarchives.gov.uk/

Section 21 of the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) is an absolute 
exemption that allows public authorities to refuse a request if the 
requested information is already reasonably accessible to the applicant 
by other means. This avoids duplicating effort and prevents authorities 
from acting as personal research services.

c) I would suggest that you access the Llandough Community Council's 
website for historical information about the community of Llandough - 
web-link is :

https://www.llandough-cc.co.uk/Buildings_of_Significance_in_our_Community_25590.aspx

Kind regards,

Paul R. Egan BA, Chartered MCIPD, CiLCA, F. Inst. LM, FIPSM

Hi Mike,

Appreciate the reply.

I kindly request an internal review of the response provided under ATISN
27021.

I am grateful for the release of the two inspection photographs dated 29
July 1988. However, I am not satisfied that the searches undertaken were
sufficient to establish that no other relevant records are held or can be
accounted for.

The response states that Great House Farm was visited and assessed for
listing by Cadw inspectors, but that the only surviving records are two
photographs. It further states that any associated records may have been
transferred to the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments
of Wales or destroyed under the Public Records Act 1958.

I respectfully submit that this conclusion appears difficult to reconcile
with the contemporary evidence.

Contemporary newspaper reports from December 1988 record that:

Cadw was actively considering emergency listing ("spot-listing") procedures
in relation to Great House Farm;

Cadw inspectors visited the site;
Cadw assessed the architectural and archaeological significance of the
property;
Cadw communicated a decision that the building did not warrant statutory
protection.

These activities would ordinarily be expected to generate records such as
inspection notes, recommendations, assessments, correspondence, memoranda,
listing files, briefing notes, internal communications, or decision records.

In addition, a surviving family witness who was present during the
inspection recalls that a written assessment was produced and supplied to
the family. The witness recalls that the assessment concluded that,
although the site was old, the building had undergone substantial
alteration over the centuries and was therefore not considered sufficiently
significant for listing.

This recollection appears broadly consistent with the reasoning attributed
to Cadw in contemporary press reports.
I therefore request clarification of the following:

Were searches undertaken for inspection notes, site notes, assessment
reports, recommendations, listing files, briefing papers, internal
memoranda, correspondence, and decision records relating to Great House
Farm?
Were accession records, transfer schedules, disposal schedules, or archive
catalogues searched to determine whether such records once existed?

If records were transferred to RCAHMW, please identify any transfer
references, accession numbers, file references, or other metadata recording
that transfer.
If records were destroyed, please identify the disposal authority,
retention schedule, and date of destruction.

If no written assessment, recommendation, report, or decision record ever
existed, please explain how Cadw reached and communicated conclusions
regarding the architectural and archaeological significance of the property.

I am not seeking reconsideration of the 1988 listing decision itself.
Rather, I seek clarification regarding the apparent absence of records
relating to a matter that was publicly reported at the time as being under
active consideration by Cadw and which resulted in a communicated decision.

Thank you for undertaking an internal review.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergenant)
Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional
Life Member of the Royal Signals

Thank you for your emails received 5-8 June.

Llandough came under Cardiff Rural District Council, 1875-1974. The plans held here have been listed and are available to search on our catalogue . There are no plans listed for Great House Farm. After this date the area come under Vale of Glamorgan Borough Council. Although some records are held for the council (catalogue available here: DCVG ) these do not include plans. No plans have been deposited by either Vale of Glamorgan Borough Council or its successor authority Vale of Glamorgan County Borough Council. We suggest that you contact them directly: planning@valeofglamorgan. gov.uk .

Correspondence received from the farm may have been reported during committee meetings: Vale of Glamorgan County Borough Council can be viewed online: CVG , and Vale of Glamorgan Borough Council: DCVG .

We do not hold any records of BP Properties Ltd or BP Pension Trust. The BP Archive (1840-2001) is held at Warwick University, and can be contacted: [email redacted] 

A catalogue to the Bute Estate records held here can be searched: DB .

Tithe maps can be searched online: Tithe Maps of Wales - Home .

Rate valuation books, 1956-1992 are here: DCVG/T/1 

There is a small Western Ground Rents Ltd Collection, consisting of three volumes, c1938-1944: D696 . However, a search of our catalogue for ‘Western Ground Rents’ will help you to locate records throughout our collections, searching for ‘Western Ground Rents AND Thomas’ may help you to identify records relating to the agreement with Daniel Thomas. A similar method can be employed to combine other search terms which will help you to identify records of relevance to your search.

If you have not visited us before you will be required to register; for this we ask you bring along two forms of identification - one showing your name (e.g. driving licence, passport) and another showing your address (e.g. a recent bill or official letter).

I hope you find this information useful.

Yours sincerely,

Hannah Price

Good afternoon,

Thank you for your further enquiry. I have checked the accessions information for the archive items which we hold related to the site. Unfortunately, there is no accessions data for the items in the NMR Site File collection. This is because most of the information was either created (in the case of notes and drawing from site visits) or collected (in the case of the newspaper cuttings) by RCAHMW staff in the course of their duties. Having examined the records themselves, however, I do note that Archive Number 6048942 may have come from a Mrs Buckler (‘Mrs Buckler?’ is handwritten under the account). There is also a note at the bottom of Archive Number 6048945 that ‘Correspondence between C.N. Johns and Mrs Buckler, Great House Farm, has been lost since 1986/87’, although I have been unable to find any other record of this correspondence either in our records or our archive catalogue, having carried out both digital and physical searches, including searching through the RCAHMW administrative files in the archive (some of which are not yet open to the public).

With regard to the first three records in the list, I include what accessions details are available below:
Archive Number
creator or originating body
accession source
accession date
6524751
Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust
Donation
20/03/2019
6416853
 Cotswold Archaeology
Donation
30/05/2014
6500905
Dr Katherine Watson
Transferred from Historic England as part of an exchange of material between the two organisations
15/01/2018

With regards to which records mention things like ownership and the dispute, most of the newspaper article clippings naturally discuss it. Archive Number 6048942 provides a short history of the site and notes the family’s residence there and Archive Number 6048945 notes that ‘The house remained partially recorded because of problems created by an ownership dispute. The house and farm buildings were suddenly and completely destroyed by B. P. Properties Ltd. on 6th December 1988 amid considerable local controversy’. If you would like further details about the content of these records, they can be viewed in our Search Room, located in the National Library of Wales, which is open Tuesday through Thursday. Scans of records can also be requested, using the attached order form. We also do offer a limited document summary service. Please see our price list for details.

In addition to these 14 records, we may hold some historical aerial photography which may include the site. This would likely include vertical aerial photography taken from a high altitude by the Royal Air Force and/or Ordnance survey from the 1940s to the turn of the 21st century. If you would like to request a search of our historic aerial photography collections, please provide details for your search, such as any location or time-period parameters. Please note that we do charge for these searches. Please see the attached price list for details.

Sincerely,

Adam Coward

Thank you for your enquiry. As noted in my email of 26 November last, while we cannot advise you on a legal case or undertake a review of historical decisions, we do hold information and archives related to Great House Farm, Llandough.

The site entry and description for the site in the National Monuments Record of Wales can be seen online on Coflein, here: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182.

We hold 14 archives related to the site, a list of which can be seen here: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182/archives?size=25. These archives can be viewed in our Search Room, located in the National Library of Wales, which is open Tuesday through Thursday, 9:30-16:30. If you would like to view the material in person, I would advise arranging with us beforehand so that we can prepare the material ahead of your visit. Some of the material is on microfiche and as we do not have a microfiche reader in the Search Room, we will need to liaise with the National Library Reading Room staff to try to negotiate the use of their machines ahead of your visit. However, I have located an electronic copy of Archive Number 6524751, which can be accessed here: https://www.walesher1974.org/her/app/php/herumd.php?group=GGAT&level=3&docid=301361628

While it is possible to order scans of material using the attached order form, we may be unable to provide research-quality scans or photographs of some of the material, such as the material on microfiche, which would require high-resolution scanning at a cost of £20 per scan. Moreover,  many of these records remain under third-party copyright, and we would only be able to provide scans or copies for personal, non-commercial research. Other uses, such as use in a legal case or report would likely require the permission of the copyright holder(s). I would therefore advise arranging to view the material in person rather than ordering scans, if possible.

Finally, I have confirmed with our Records Manager that we do not hold any correspondence related to the site.

Thank you again for your enquiry.

Sincerely,

Adam Coward

Dear Mr Buckler

The Council's Information Governance Team works collaboratively, and requests are managed collectively across the team rather than by individual officers. For this reason, correspondence is not issued under individual names. The team is managed by Evelyn Morgan who is the Council's Data Protection Officer/Information Manager.

We appreciate the detailed correspondence you have provided to date and understand that this matter is of importance to you. We have received multiple items of correspondence from you, including earlier requests relating to the legal case of BP Properties Ltd v Buckler. Work had already been undertaken to review this request and we were in the process of preparing a response when your more recent correspondence was received. We were aiming to ensure that all appropriate lines of enquiry had been explored before providing a response.

At this stage, we would like to clarify that the Vale of Glamorgan Council does not hold records relating to this historic legal matter. Neither the Council nor its predecessor authorities, the Vale of Glamorgan Borough Council or the former South Glamorgan County Council were involved in the case of BP Properties Ltd v Buckler. From the information available, it appears this was a private legal matter between BP Properties Ltd and the Buckler family. We also recognise that your enquiries extend beyond the Council and have been shared with a number of organisations. Some of the information you are seeking is more likely to be held elsewhere and not with the Council. Some information that may have historically been retained by the Council may now be held by the Glamorgan Archives but only in relation to historical land ownership, tenancy records, or court administrative deposits. Some information may also be obtainable from the Land Registry, but we can see that they have been included in your correspondence.

In terms of information the Council may hold, this is most likely limited to planning related records. As previously advised, in order for our Planning colleagues to conduct accurate searches, they have requested a copy of the relevant site plan. Without this, there is a risk that any searches undertaken may not capture all relevant records.  We note that this does not mean there are records just that in trying to cover every possibility we have asked for a site plan to complete this aspect of our enquiries.  There may not be anything held but, we are trying to search for you.  It is entirely a matter for you as to whether you provide a site plan. If you do not wish to provide one you do not have to but that will restrict our enquiries as it will be difficult to pin down the correct area.

We are looking to assist in providing you with a full response as soon as possible with the information that is held by the Council. Your cooperation in providing the requested plan will help us progress this matter efficiently.

We look forward to hearing from you.

Kind regards

Dear Freedom of Information Officer,
RE: Information Request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the Environmental Information Regulations 2004
I am writing to request access to historical records, internal correspondence, planning briefs, and assessments held by your organization regarding Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth/Cardiff (demolished December 1988), and the historical occupancy of the Buckler family.
Statutory Mandate on Accessibility & Charging Fees:
I am aware that previous attempts to locate this data have resulted in directives to visit physical archives in person or use paywalled, commercial third-party web portals. Please be advised of the following statutory obligations:

  1.  Under EIR Regulation 8, fees cannot act as an unreasonable barrier or deterrent to access. Because my family was historically displaced from this site and I am executing this request remotely, forcing physical attendance or demanding payment constitutes an unlawful obstacle.
  2.  Public authorities are required to supply information in the format requested. I require all documents to be delivered digitally via email attachment or secure electronic download link, free of charge, as specified by the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) guidelines for data already held electronically.
Please provide all recorded information matching the following points:
1. Tenant/Ownership Identification and the 1880 Report

  *   Any documents, archival notes, or registry indexes citing the William/ Buckler family line (who occupied and farmed the house across four generations).
  *   Clarification on whether my family members were formally cited as the legal owners, long-term tenants, or registered reporters of the 1880 discovery under the dining room floor.
  *   Any explicit records indicating gaps, deleted metadata, or missing volumes in your authority's archive concerning the tenancy, land-dispute maps, or agricultural heritage of Great House Farm between 1950 and 1989.
2. Statutory Protection and Cadw's Assessments

  *   Given that the site's extreme archaeological value (a 1st-to-4th-century Roman precursor villa and a massive early medieval monastic settlement) was verified by rescue operations as early as 1979, what are the recorded reasons why Cadw failed to place a statutory Schedule or Protection Order on the standing fabric of Great House Farm before its demolition?
  *   All internal correspondence, risk assessments, or ministerial briefs evaluating the preservation value of the sub-medieval direct-entry farmhouse core before it was levelled.
3. Planning Approvals and Local Authority Governance

  *   All minutes, planning committee files, and consultation responses from the local authority that granted planning permission and housing development rights on this specific acreage.
  *   Direct information explaining how the council approved planning permission for a private housing development in light of the documented historical evidence surrounding the immediate parish boundary.
4. Institutional Concealment and Historical "Ignorance"

  *   Records showing exactly where and at what stage of the planning process this archaeological evidence should have been brought up but was not, which ultimately allowed developers and public bodies to claim they were unaware of the land's deep significance until after the farmhouse was destroyed and housing development began.
  *   Any environmental impact assessments, historic environment register (HER) lookups, or developer briefs filed between 1980 and 1990 regarding the footprint of Great House Farm.
If any part of this request is refused under the guise of commercial sensitivity or archival limitations, you are required by law to state the exact statutory exemption applied and provide a formal internal review pathway.
I expect your response within the statutory 20-working-day timeframe.

LEGAL NOTICE TO RECIPIENTS:
*Take notice that this request is issued in anticipation of formal legal
proceedings and the filing of an official report regarding systemic
institutional fraud, land misconduct, and the unlawful concealment of
historic preservation data. You are under a strict legal duty to preserve
all physical and electronic records, metadata, correspondence, maps, and
erased files relating to this site. Any spoliation, deletion, or
withholding of data will be cited in subsequent court filings.*
Dear Freedom of Information Officer,
RE: Information Request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the
Environmental Information Regulations 2004
I am writing to request access to historical records, internal
correspondence, planning briefs, and assessments held by your organization
regarding Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth/Cardiff (demolished
December 1988), and the historical occupancy of the Buckler family.
Statutory Mandate on Accessibility & Charging Fees:
I am aware that previous attempts to locate this data have resulted in
directives to visit physical archives in person or use paywalled,
commercial third-party web portals. Please be advised of the following
statutory obligations:

   1. Under EIR Regulation 8, fees cannot act as an unreasonable barrier or
   deterrent to access. Because my family was historically displaced from this
   site and I am executing this request remotely, forcing physical attendance
   or demanding payment constitutes an unlawful obstacle.
   2. Public authorities are required to supply information in the format
   requested. I require all documents to be delivered digitally via email
   attachment or secure electronic download link, free of charge, as
   specified by the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) guidelines for
   data already held electronically.

Please provide all recorded information matching the following points:
1. Tenant/Ownership Identification and the 1880 Report

   - Any documents, archival notes, or registry indexes citing the
William/ Buckler
   family line (who occupied and farmed the house across four generations).
   - Clarification on whether my family members were formally cited as the
   legal owners, long-term tenants, or registered reporters of the 1880
   discovery under the dining room floor.
   - Any explicit records indicating gaps, deleted metadata, or missing
   volumes in your authority’s archive concerning the tenancy, land-dispute
   maps, or agricultural heritage of Great House Farm between 1950 and 1989.

2. Statutory Protection and Cadw’s Assessments

   - Given that the site's extreme archaeological value (a
   1st-to-4th-century Roman precursor villa and a massive early medieval
   monastic settlement) was verified by rescue operations as early as 1979,
   what are the recorded reasons why Cadw failed to place a statutory
   Schedule or Protection Order on the standing fabric of Great House Farm
   before its demolition?
   - All internal correspondence, risk assessments, or ministerial briefs
   evaluating the preservation value of the sub-medieval direct-entry
   farmhouse core before it was levelled.

3. Planning Approvals and Local Authority Governance

   - All minutes, planning committee files, and consultation responses from
   the local authority that granted planning permission and housing
   development rights on this specific acreage.
   - Direct information explaining how the council approved planning
   permission for a private housing development in light of the documented
   historical evidence surrounding the immediate parish boundary.

4. Institutional Concealment and Historical "Ignorance"

   - Records showing exactly where and at what stage of the planning
   process this archaeological evidence should have been brought up
but was not,
   which ultimately allowed developers and public bodies to claim they were
   unaware of the land's deep significance until after the farmhouse was
   destroyed and housing development began.
   - Any environmental impact assessments, historic environment register
   (HER) lookups, or developer briefs filed between 1980 and 1990 regarding
   the footprint of Great House Farm.

If any part of this request is refused under the guise of commercial
sensitivity or archival limitations, you are required by law to state the
exact statutory exemption applied and provide a formal internal review
pathway.
I expect your response within the statutory 20-working-day timeframe.
Kind regards,
*Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*
*[address redacted], Dinas Powys, Vale of Glamorgan*

Good afternoon,

Thank you for your enquiry. As noted in my email of 26 November last, while we cannot advise you on a legal case or undertake a review of historical decisions, we do hold information and archives related to Great House Farm, Llandough.

The site entry and description for the site in the National Monuments Record of Wales can be seen online on Coflein, here: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182.

We hold 14 archives related to the site, a list of which can be seen here: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182/archives?size=25. These archives can be viewed in our Search Room, located in the National Library of Wales, which is open Tuesday through Thursday, 9:30-16:30. If you would like to view the material in person, I would advise arranging with us beforehand so that we can prepare the material ahead of your visit. Some of the material is on microfiche and as we do not have a microfiche reader in the Search Room, we will need to liaise with the National Library Reading Room staff to try to negotiate the use of their machines ahead of your visit. However, I have located an electronic copy of Archive Number 6524751, which can be accessed here: https://www.walesher1974.org/her/app/php/herumd.php?group=GGAT&level=3&docid=301361628

While it is possible to order scans of material using the attached order form, we may be unable to provide research-quality scans or photographs of some of the material, such as the material on microfiche, which would require high-resolution scanning at a cost of £20 per scan. Moreover,  many of these records remain under third-party copyright, and we would only be able to provide scans or copies for personal, non-commercial research. Other uses, such as use in a legal case or report would likely require the permission of the copyright holder(s). I would therefore advise arranging to view the material in person rather than ordering scans, if possible.

Finally, I have confirmed with our Records Manager that we do not hold any correspondence related to the site.

Thank you again for your enquiry.

Sincerely,

Adam Coward

Thank you for your response dated 25 May 2026 regarding title WA231076.

I note your statement that HM Land Registry considered my grandmother to be
the same individual despite the use of different surnames and that “there
is a marriage certificate to show this”.

Please could you clarify:

   1. Was a marriage certificate actually lodged with HM Land Registry as
   part of the registration evidence relied upon by HM Land Registry, or are
   you referring to information held elsewhere?
   2. If such a certificate formed part of the registration evidence
   considered by HM Land Registry, please identify the document relied upon
   and whether copies may be requested.
   3. Prior correspondence and BP licence letters before 1974, to my
   understanding, referred to my grandmother as Mrs Williams. I am therefore
   trying to understand the evidential chain relied upon and how identity
   continuity was established.

I also wish to clarify that my purpose has been to query and understand the
historical record and registration process. I did not submit this as a
complaint; my intention was to seek clarification and challenge aspects of
the historical narrative where I believe evidence may be incomplete or
disputed.

My concerns extend beyond the surname issue. I remain concerned about
whether all appropriate checks and safeguards were applied at the time of
registration and whether the underlying evidence was fully scrutinised.

I understand HM Land Registry’s position that it records interests
presented to it and is not a forum for determining disputes. However, I am
still gathering evidence and attempting to understand how these events
occurred and whether any procedural irregularities existed.

At present I am not asking HM Land Registry to accept my conclusions. I am
requesting transparency regarding the evidence and process relied upon.

Thank you again for your reply.

Regards,

Sion Buckler

To whom it may concern,

I am writing as the child of Branwen and William (“Billy”) Buckler
regarding the destruction of Great House Farm, Llandough, and the
long-running dispute surrounding BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987].

I have compiled a substantial historical archive, including newspaper
reports, court references, family testimony, archaeological material,
estate history, and public records relating to Great House Farm (“Ty
Mawr”), a site associated with medieval, monastic, and Roman occupation.

The archive is currently being made into a website at:

bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz

The material raises serious unresolved questions regarding:

• The treatment of us Williams/Buckler family’s longstanding occupation and
asserted ownership claims. • The repeated use of possession proceedings
without a full adjudication of superior title. • Missing or allegedly
suppressed title documentation connected to Bute estate transfers and later
transactions. • The demolition of an allegedly medieval structure during an
active heritage controversy. • Whether the archaeological significance of
the site was fully disclosed during planning and demolition processes. •
The wider public interest and cultural significance of the site and its
destruction.

It's looking to me like my family actually did obtain fee simple absolute
and manorial title. Then it was stolen and attempts were made by the
possessor of the stolen title, to make my family lessee's / tenants as we
were when we were on the virtual freehold (999 year lease) aquired in 1667.
Thereafter it appears to be a death of a thousand cuts of proceedural
unfairness, audacity, fraud, court "mistakes" , purgery and more.

https://youtu.be/4GXmR7mAas0?feature=shared

Contemporaneous newspaper coverage from the 1970s and 1980s demonstrates
that these concerns were publicly known at the time, including heritage
objections, petitions, and public claims of ancestral ownership.

I am requesting:

   1. Review and preservation consideration of all surviving records
   connected to Great House Farm.
   2. Clarification as to whether any formal heritage review or
   investigation into the demolition process was ever completed.
   3. Guidance regarding access to archival and planning materials relevant
   to the site.
   4. Consideration of whether this matter warrants renewed historical or
   heritage examination.

I appreciate that some claims remain disputed or unproven, and I am not
asking recipients to accept every allegation as established fact. However,
I believe the totality of the historical material warrants serious review
rather than dismissal.

I would be grateful for acknowledgement of receipt and guidance on the
appropriate next steps.

Kind regards,


Sion Buckler Esq. (Ret'd Sergeant)

Manor of Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan

I write to append further evidence and clarification to my ongoing
complaint regarding the registration of title relating to Great House Farm,
Llandough (also known as Ty Mawr / Great House).

https://youtu.be/4GXmR7mAas0?feature=shared

This submission sets out a series of facts which I can evidence and which,
taken together, raise serious concerns of fraud, concealment, and wrongful
registration that have materially affected the rights of the Williams
family and their heirs.

1. Unauthorised transfer of title (circa 1965)
I can evidence that the title to the property was transferred or sold in or
around 1965 by Frederick Buckler without the knowledge or consent of Mrs
Mary Williams, who maintained a rightful claim to the property. This raises
the issue that the disposition may have been made without lawful authority.

2. Death of key party and concealment (1968)
Frederick Buckler died in 1968. Any knowledge he held regarding the
circumstances of the transfer died with him, preventing proper scrutiny or
challenge at the time.

3. Inability to prove ownership in court (1974)
Mrs Mary Williams was subsequently unable to prove her claim in court
proceedings in 1974. This inability must be viewed in the context of the
prior undisclosed transfer and the absence of key evidence and testimony.

4. Knowledge of defective title by acquiring party
There is a credible basis to assert that the acquiring party (BP and/or its
associated property entities) knew, or ought reasonably to have known, that
the title they acquired was defective. This point is central and I am
compiling supporting material demonstrating notice and/or constructive
knowledge.

5. Registration following death of claimant
Mrs Mary Williams died prior to the land being formally registered in the
name of the acquiring party. As a result, she was denied any opportunity to
rebut, challenge, or correct the position before registration was effected.

6. Death of additional disputing party
Mr Buckler also died during the period in which he was engaged in disputing
the matter. The cumulative effect is that all primary individuals with
direct knowledge were deceased before the issue could be fully and fairly
resolved.

7. Ongoing family claim
Despite these events, the claim of the Williams family has never been
relinquished. The position remains that the title was wrongfully
transferred and subsequently registered on the basis of that defective
transfer.

---

Request for Action

In light of the above, I respectfully request that:

1. This evidence be formally appended to my existing complaint file.
2. The register be reviewed in accordance with provisions relating to
fraud, mistake, and/or rectification.
3. Consideration be given to whether the registration was obtained through
or affected by fraud or concealment.
4. I be informed of the appropriate process for seeking rectification
and/or indemnity.

I am prepared to provide supporting documents, including historical
records, press reports, and family documentation, upon request or via
secure submission.

Given the seriousness of the matters raised, I would be grateful for
written confirmation that this submission has been received and attached to
my complaint, along with an outline of the next steps.

Yours faithfully,


Sion Buckler

Ms Hollis,

I write further to your letter of 27 April 2026. This correspondence
constitutes formal pre-action notice of my intention to pursue legal
remedies arising from the historic proceedings concerning Great House Farm,
Llandough.

While I note your position regarding judicial independence, I do not accept
that the issues raised can be dismissed at an administrative level. My
representations concern alleged fraud, procedural irregularity,
misrepresentation, non-disclosure, and structural unfairness which, taken
together, raise serious questions as to whether the proceedings to
dispossess my disabled, widowed nan, of our land and farm since 1667, as
indigenous Welsh Britons on iur ancestral birthland, were properly and
fairly determined. Removing us with 30 police doesn't mean we surrender our
superior land claim. And the fraud I discovered this year is the beginning
of the Limitation clock so far as I understand, despite the fraud occuring
almost 40 years ago. Fraud unravels all. ALL!

These matters warrant proper consideration, or at minimum clear direction
to an appropriate forum capable of examining them.
------------------------------
A. Grounds for Reparations

The basis upon which reparations are sought includes:

   - Continuous occupation over approximately 318 years (1667–1988), open,
   peaceful, and without permission (*nec vi, nec clam, nec precario*),
   establishing de facto ownership;
   - No voluntary surrender of rights at any stage, with the claim
   maintained consistently to the present day;
   - Uncompensated dispossession, including eviction and demolition without
   settlement;
   - Coercive enforcement measures, including forced removal, detention,
   restraining measures, and demolition under duress;
   - The rendering of a vulnerable family homeless, including a pregnant
   mother, young children, and a disabled elderly occupant;
   - Ongoing intergenerational harm, including psychological, social, and
   economic consequences;
   - Destruction of an ancestral home of significant age and character
   (approximately 800 years);
   - Loss or disappearance of family records and evidential materials
   relevant to ownership;
   - Failure to act upon known archaeological and historical significance,
   resulting in loss of heritage protection;
   - Resulting public interest harm through the destruction of a site of
   historical importance.

------------------------------
B. Grounds to Set Aside or Reopen the 1987 Ruling 1. Reliance on a disputed
“licence by silence”

The judgment relied upon an inferred licence accepted through silence. This
is unsafe where:

   - correspondence was addressed to a disputed identity (“Mrs Buckler”);
   - evidence of active rejection (including 1978 news paper article) was
   not before the court.

2. Identity misrepresentation

Mary Williams was treated as “Mrs Buckler,” which:

   - did not reflect her asserted identity;
   - weakened her position by obscuring lineage-based claims;
   - artificially linked her to the alleged intent of another party.

3. Misplaced reliance on Frederick Buckler’s intent

Any alleged intention:

   - was personal to him and legally distinct;
   - did not bind Mary Williams;
   - was extinguished upon his death in 1965;
   - and was not supported by fulfilment of tenancy obligations.

4. Procedural irregularities (1974)

There are serious concerns that:

   - an appeal attempt and request for a stay were disrupted;
   - licence correspondence was timed and/or presented so as to defeat due
   process;
   - a key hearing was effectively neutralised before determination.

5. Non-disclosure of material facts

Relevant matters appear not to have been disclosed, including:

   - evidence of public rejection of the opposing claim;
   - archaeological and historical significance of the site;
   - the existence of an ongoing dispute in the context of land
   registration.

6. Inconsistent treatment of corporate identity

   - In 1987, my grandmother’s rebuttal to BP Pension Trust was disregarded
   on the basis that BP Pension Trust and BP Properties were separate entities;
   - In subsequent proceedings, the same entities were treated as
   effectively the same when dismissing an appeal.

This inconsistency materially affected the outcome and raises concerns as
to fairness and legal coherence.
7. Avoidance of substantive title determination

The case proceeded within a possession framework rather than determining
underlying ownership in an appropriate forum, resulting in the absence of a
definitive adjudication on title.
8. Possible misrepresentation / constructive fraud

Concerns arise that:

   - licence arrangements were asserted under a disputed identity;
   - the authority of the issuing entity was unclear;
   - planning and property descriptions may have mischaracterised the
   nature of the building.

9. New or previously unavailable evidence

This includes:

   - missing or unavailable title documentation;
   - evidence relating to arrangements (including that attributed to Daniel
   Thomas);
   - family testimony not previously considered;
   - subsequent archaeological findings supporting the site’s significance.

------------------------------
C. Core Position

Taken together, the 1987 outcome is arguable as unsafe due to flawed
assumptions, missing evidence, and procedural unfairness. The resulting
dispossession, demolition, and long-term harm give rise to a basis for
reparative consideration.
------------------------------
D. Why the Matter Requires Proper Consideration

This matter should not be dismissed solely on the basis of judicial
independence because:

   - The issues raised concern the *integrity of the process*, not simply
   disagreement with a result;
   - Allegations of *misrepresentation, non-disclosure, and procedural
   irregularity* fall outside ordinary appellate disagreement;
   - There is a *public interest dimension*, including loss of heritage and
   potential systemic issues;
   - The passage of time does not extinguish claims where *fraud or
   material injustice* is alleged;
   - Clarification is required as to the appropriate forum capable of
   examining such matters.

------------------------------
E. Request for Clarification

Before commencing proceedings, I request clarification of the following:

   1. Whether any formal mechanism exists within government for referring
   allegations of procedural irregularity or fraud in historic cases for
   independent review;
   2. Whether my correspondence has been referred to any oversight or
   investigatory body;
   3. Whether the Ministry maintains any position as to the appropriate
   route for consideration of such evidence outside of direct court
   proceedings.

------------------------------

Please treat this letter as a formal pre-action notice. I would be grateful
for a substantive response within 14 days.

Nothing in this letter should be taken as a waiver of any rights or
remedies, all of which are expressly reserved.

Yours sincerely,


Sion Buckler Esq. (Ret'd Sgt)

Manor of Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan

Sir or Madam,

I write to ask that my complaint regarding title number WA231076 (Land on
the North Side of Leckwith Road, Llandough) be escalated to **stage two**
of HM Land Registry’s Complaints Procedure. This email sets out why I
consider the stage‑one decision to be incorrect, identifies the mistake I
say exists in the register, and explains the decision I seek.

### 1. My core contention

My core contention is that BP Properties Limited were registered as
proprietors on the basis of a factual and legal error regarding my
grandmother’s status on the land. My grandmother did not occupy under any
genuine licence granted to her and did not relinquish any claim. Instead,
any licence relied on by BP related to a different name/person. As her
heir, I have succeeded to her claim; I therefore say that registering BP as
proprietors was a “mistake in the register” for the purposes of the Land
Registration Act 2002.

### 2. Identity mismatch and alleged “licence”

Your stage‑one letter records that HM Land Registry relies on the Court of
Appeal decision in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler  EWCA Civ 2, and treats my
grandmother as having occupied under a licence granted by the documentary
title holder, so that her possession was no longer adverse.

However, the alleged licence and related correspondence did not use my
grandmother’s true legal name. My grandmother was Mrs Williams (supported
by her birth, marriage and death certificates), not “Mrs Buckler”. The
“licensee” referred to in BP’s narrative and in the 1987 litigation is
therefore not the same legal person as my grandmother. There is, in other
words, a fundamental mis‑identification or identity fraud at the heart of
the story that HM Land Registry and the Court have relied upon.

If the licence relied on by BP was addressed to, or granted in respect of,
a different named individual, it cannot properly be said that my
grandmother’s occupation was under that licence. In that case her
occupation remained adverse to BP’s paper title, and any finding that she
was a “licensee” rests on a factual premise that is demonstrably wrong.

### 3. Timing – “cart before the horse”

Your letter explains that the applications for first registration of
WA231076 (and the related title WA240304) were made in 1982–83 and that BP
demonstrated a documentary root of title back to 1969/1975 by way of
conveyances and a 1971 abstract of title.

You also confirm that the Court of Appeal only gave its decision in BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler in 1987, holding that an offer by BP to let my
grandmother remain created a licence and brought her adverse possession to
an end.

This highlights a fundamental sequencing problem:

- At the date of first registration (1982–83), whether there was a valid
licence capable of defeating my grandmother’s adverse possession was a
live, unresolved dispute.
- BP nevertheless presented themselves as entitled to be registered as
proprietors and their solicitors certified on form FR1 that there was no
question or doubt affecting the title.

- HM Land Registry, relying on that certification, registered BP before any
court had determined whether my grandmother’s possession had extinguished
BP’s title.
- Only in 1987 did the Court of Appeal retrospectively treat the alleged
licence as bringing adverse possession to an end, and that decision was
itself based on the mis‑identification described above.

In simple terms, the effect of the alleged licence (if any) was judicially
determined **after** first registration, and on the basis of the wrong
person being treated as the “licensee”. BP and their solicitors put the
cart before the horse, and HM Land Registry accepted that position.

### 4. The specific “mistake in the register”

Your stage‑one response concludes that there is “no evidence of a mistake
in the register” and therefore no power to alter the register and no right
to indemnity. I say this is incorrect.

The mistake I allege is as follows:

1. On the true facts, my grandmother’s occupation of the land was adverse
to BP’s documentary title and was not under any valid licence granted to
her.

2. Her adverse possession had, or may have, extinguished BP’s title by the
time of first registration in 1982–83, meaning BP were not entitled to be
registered as proprietors at that time.

3. HM Land Registry nevertheless registered BP as proprietors on the basis
of:
   - a licence attributed to the wrong person (identity error/fraud), and
   - a solicitor’s FR1 certificate stating there was no question or doubt
affecting title, despite a long‑running dispute and pending litigation.

4. Subsequent reliance on the 1987 Court of Appeal decision does not cure
this, because that decision itself proceeded on the mis‑identification of
my grandmother and did not and could not retrospectively validate a licence
that never related to her.

On that analysis, the register shows BP as proprietors when, in law, my
grandmother’s adverse possession should have extinguished BP’s title and
given rise to a transmissible proprietary interest which I, as her heir,
now claim. The register therefore does not accurately reflect the true
legal position and contains a mistake capable of rectification.

### 5. Why the stage‑one reasoning is inadequate

In your stage‑one letter you state that:

- HM Land Registry has an administrative function and cannot “look behind
or challenge decisions of the Court”. [1]
- My identity‑fraud claims are “not relevant to the issue of title to the
land” because they relate to the dispute heard by the Court.

- There is no evidence of negligence or maladministration and no evidence
of a mistake in the register.

With respect, this reasoning is incomplete:

- Once HM Land Registry is presented with clear evidence that the person
named as the “licensee” in the litigation and licence documentation is not
the same legal person as the occupier (my grandmother), that goes directly
to whether the Court of Appeal’s factual premise remains reliable and
whether the register is accurate.

- Recognising that there is a serious question as to the correctness of the
register is not the same as “overturning” the Court of Appeal. HM Land
Registry has statutory powers to alter the register where there is a
mistake, and it can, where appropriate, refer disputes about rectification
to the tribunal or the courts.

- To simply say that identity‑fraud concerns are “not relevant to title”
is, I say, an error of law and/or an unreasonable application of policy. It
disregards new evidence going to the foundation of BP’s claimed entitlement.

### 6. The decision and outcome I seek

For stage two, I ask that a Land Registrar (Senior Officer) reconsider the
complaint and:

1. Accept that the combination of:
   - the identity mismatch (licence/name vs my grandmother’s true legal
name), and
   - the timing (registration in 1982–83 before the 1987 decision) gives
rise to at least a **serious question** as to whether the register is
mistaken in showing BP/ Companies thereafter, as proprietors.

2. Treat this as evidence of a potential “mistake in the register” for the
purposes of your alteration powers and Schedule 8, rather than as a mere
disagreement with the 1987 judgment.

3. Either:

   - (a) commence the process of rectification, recognising that my
grandmother’s adverse possession may have extinguished BP’s title and that
I, as her heir, now have a claim to be registered, or

   - (b) formally refer the dispute over the correctness of the register to
the appropriate tribunal/court, making clear that HM Land Registry
recognises that the identity‑fraud evidence raises a real issue about
whether the register is accurate.

Ms Griffiths,

Thanks for your letter of 23 March 2026 regarding the historic registration
of Ty Mawr Farm, title WA231076. I note your explanation of HM Land
Registry’s administrative role and that you say there is no evidence of a
“mistake” on the basis of the file you have reviewed.

My family’s concern, however, is that the first registration was procured
by misrepresentation and identity fraud by BP, rather than by a simple
clerical error. The occupier was my grandmother, Mrs Williams, from a
family that had occupied the property and land since at least 1667, not the
fictitious “Mrs Buckler” BP fabricated in 1974 for their unilateral
licence, which was the basis of the BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1987) case.
BP also appears to have failed to disclose the long‑running ownership
dispute. In a 1978 suppressed newspaper article, my grandmother publicly
asserted her ownership and stated that BP could not prove ownership and had
never obtained a court ruling that it was the owner, only possession orders.

How was BP able to register our land in its name? Did HM Land Registry
enquire whether there was any dispute over the land, given that the dispute
appears in court records from 1974? Twice that year BP obstructed my
grandmother from making her case that she owned the land: first, the
hearing was adjourned without a ruling; then the licence letters, using
identity fraud, prevented the second hearing from taking place. These were
opportunities to dispossess a widowed, disabled woman.
Had HM Land Registry recorded or investigated the existence of this
dispute, BP’s inability to prove ownership, the archaeological and historic
significance of the site, or sought a copy of my grandmother’s death
certificate to see that the name on the licence and narrative were
completely different, we believe BP would not have been able to achieve
first registration on the basis presented. Instead, the use of the wrong
name (“Mrs Buckler” instead of my married grandmother, Mrs Williams) and
the non‑disclosure of the dispute and family claim enabled dispossession
through what we say was identity fraud, which my grandmother was unable to
contest as she also died in the same year as registration.

I wish to append to this land parcel our maintained position of dispute. We
never surrendered. We were removed by around 30 police officers and
information was suppressed. My family being paralysed by fear and silence
is not the same as surrender from sound mind and agency.
Further background is set out at bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz. My family wants
narrative justice as the possibly rightful, dispossessed via fraud,
executors of the Manor of Llandough.

I am aware that HM Land Registry operates a statutory indemnity and redress
scheme under the Land Registration Act 2002, and that substantial payments
(including around £8 million in a single year) have been made where people
suffer loss because of mistakes or fraud in the register. I therefore wish
to explore, formally, whether our family’s loss of Ty Mawr Farm, in
circumstances where BP’s misrepresentations and the suppression of an
active dispute were not reflected on the register, can be considered within
that indemnity/redress framework.

In light of the above, I ask HM Land Registry to state clearly whether you
accept or deny that:
BP was able to obtain first registration of Ty Mawr Farm even though there
was no court ruling that BP owned the land and BP had been unable to prove
ownership in proceedings, which were confined to possession.

The land was registered while there was an active and public dispute over
ownership (including my grandmother’s 1978 public assertion of ownership
and the BP v Buckler litigation), and while the long‑term occupier, my
grandmother, had died and was therefore unable to challenge the application.

My grandmother’s identity and superior family title and land claim
associated with that name were mis‑described in the material on which you
relied, as BP used “Mrs Buckler” instead of my married grandmother’s actual
name, Mrs Williams, and that this misdescription and the concealment of the
dispute were not detected or queried by HM Land Registry before completing
first registration.�
If these matters are admitted, I consider they amount to negligence and
maladministration by HM Land Registry in allowing BP to register our family
land in its name in those circumstances. If you do not accept that, please
explain precisely which of the above points you dispute and on what basis,
so that I can take appropriate legal advice and pursue an indemnity/redress
claim if available.
Separately from that, please also:
Provide official copies of the 23 May 1975 and 19 November 1982
conveyances, and of the first registration applications and all supporting
documents for WA231076 and WA240304, so I can obtain specialist advice on
the extent of any misrepresentation in what was lodged.

Confirm the correct procedure and forms to make a claim under your
indemnity/redress scheme in a historic case of alleged fraud and
misrepresentation in first registration, and whether you consider this
matter potentially falls within that scheme, subject to evidence.

I appreciate that you cannot determine the underlying ownership dispute,
but it is important that HM Land Registry notes that the Buckler/Williams
family contests the integrity of the original registration of Ty Mawr Farm
on the basis of identity fraud, non‑disclosure of a live dispute, and the
absence of any judicial determination that BP owned the land.

Regards,

Sion Buckler

If you have made a request under the Freedom of Information Act or Environmental Information Regulations – the statutory timescale for response is 20 working days following receipt of your request.

If you have made a request in relation to your data rights, for example, a subject access request for personal data – the statutory timescale for response is one calendar month following receipt of your request.

Information Rights Team
HM Land Registry

Accessing information held by HMLR on our register of title

To assist you in accessing information held by HMLR, please be aware most of the information held within our registers is open to public inspection and accessible via statutory routes of access. This means that we may be unable to provide access to this information via a Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) request.

Statutory Routes of Access to information held on Public Registers

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for keeping a register of title to land and property, and in accordance with Section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act, it is a requirement that the Chief Land Registrar makes this information (including any documents held on the register of title) available for public inspection.

How to access information held on our Registers

The information you have requested is available to access under our statutory protocol under section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act 2002.

Search for Land and Property

Please visit our website for further information about our registers:

www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land<http://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land>

Official Copies

For information about how to apply for official copies of documents held in relation to registered titles, and information about the types of documents available, please refer to practice guide 11:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

Index of proprietors’ names

Under rule 11 of the Land Registration Rules 2003 the registrar is required to keep an index of proprietors’ names which shows for each individual register the proprietor of the registered estate and the proprietor of any registered charge together with the title number. When you search the index of proprietors’ names, you will receive a list of titles that are owned by, or mortgaged to, the name that you have searched against.

For further information about this please refer to practice guide 74:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names>

Section 21 FOIA exemption: Information accessible to the applicant by other means

Where information held on the register of title is available for inspection through these statutory routes of access it is exempt from disclosure under section 21(2)(b) of FOIA.

Section 21 states:

“21 Information accessible to applicant by other means.

(1) Information which is reasonably accessible to the applicant otherwise than under section 1 is exempt information.

(2) For the purposes of subsection (1)—

(a) information may be reasonably accessible to the applicant even though it is accessible only on payment, and

(b) information is to be taken to be reasonably accessible to the applicant if it is information which the public authority or any other person is obliged by or under any enactment to communicate (otherwise than by making the information available for inspection) to members of the public on request, whether free of charge or on payment.”

Therefore, we are unable to provide information held on our register through FOIA, as it covered by this exemption.

Advice and assistance

Under Section 16 of FOIA and in accordance with the Section 45 FOIA code of practice, we have a duty to provide you with reasonable advice and assistance.

Please note that the ICO has previously reviewed HM Land Registry’s use of the section 21 exemption. Relevant decision notices can be accessed here<https://icosearch.ico.org.uk/s/search.html?collection=ico-meta&profile=decisions&query&query=&f.By+authority%7CpublicAuthority=HM%20Land%20Registry&f.By+section%7CsectionOfLegislation=FOI%2021> including IC-173302-N4J1<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2022/4022883/ic-173302-n4j1.pdf>, FS50685812<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2017/2172810/fs50685812.pdf> and FER0454056<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2012/780474/fer_0454056.pdf>.

The ICO has agreed that this position is long established, and the Commissioner is satisfied that section 21 would be engaged for this type of request.

For assistance on how to obtain official copies of documents you can contact our Customer Support Centre by telephone between 8am and 5pm, Monday to Thursday on [phone redacted] or online through our Contact Us<https://customerhelp.landregistry.gov.uk/guide-page-external/?stepid=2b31bc48-eb96-eb11-b1ac-002248413956> form.

Our Customer Support colleagues are trained to handle queries which relate to information that is held on the register of title.

Information about how to apply to inspect or obtain official copies is contained with practice guide 11:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

If you need any support completing the application form for official copies or to determine which documents to order, you may contact our Customer Support colleagues:

www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry>

You may also refer to our Publication Scheme which includes information about how to access information that is held on the register of title under the heading ‘Request information’:

www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/publication-scheme#request-information<http://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/publication-scheme#request-information>

Please refer to HMLR’s Transaction Data webpage which contains information in respect of commonly used abbreviations:

www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-transaction-data#abbreviations-used-in-transaction-data<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-transaction-data#abbreviations-used-in-transaction-data>

If you need any independent advice about individual’s rights under information legislation you can contact the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). The ICO is the UK’s independent authority set up to uphold information rights in the public interest, promoting openness by public bodies and data privacy for individuals.

The contact details for the ICO are detailed below. There is useful information on the ICO website which explains the rights of individuals:

www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public<http://www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public>

Please refer to the top tips:

www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public/official-information<http://www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public/official-information/>

Register information and your data protection rights

Data protection law permits HM Land Registry to use personal data for our official purposes.

The lawful basis for HM Land Registry processing personal data under the United Kingdom (UK) General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) is that it is necessary to enable us to perform our public task of the registration of land and property (Article 6(1)(e) of UK GDPR). This is defined in the Land Registration Act 2002.

Paragraph 5 of Schedule 2 Part 1 of the Data Protection Act 2018 provides the following exemption from the specified UK GDPR provisions:

“The listed UK GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for the keeping of a register of title to land and requirements for its administration by HM Land Registry under a Chief Land Registrar.

The Chief Land Registrar is required by the Land Registration Act 2002 and to make register information (including any documents held on the register of title) available to the public, therefore the following data protection provisions do not apply:


  *   the requirement to provide ‘privacy notices’ to individuals
  *   the requirement to provide personal data in response to subject access requests
  *   the requirement to rectification
  *   the requirement to comply with requests to erasure (right to be ‘forgotten’)
  *   most of the principles of UK GDPR

> arises from an agreement between John Williams (occupier of Great House
> Farm / Ty Mawr / Cedfin) and Daniel Thomas & Son (Bute Estate quarry
> operators / limestoners). In essence, the Williams family granted
> permission for quarrying on part of the farm in return for equitable title
> / permanent security of tenure once quarrying was complete. Daniel Thomas
> is said to have formalised his side by a land-swap deed with the Bute
> Estate (copy formerly held in Cardiff Library, now reported missing along
> with its index card in 1984).
>
> This places the key transaction squarely in the early 20th-century Bute
> estate rationalisation period, immediately before the 1916 agricultural
> tenancy to John Williams and the 1915 death of Daniel Thomas (after which
> Bute attempted eviction, only for the equitable interest to be asserted
> successfully at the time). Family testimony, supported by the 1876
> limeworks severance (Glamorgan Archives D153/4-8) and the known industrial
> quarrying context, points to this narrow window as the origin of the modern
> title dispute.
>
> *Why this matters now* The 1987 Court of Appeal decision (*BP Properties
> Ltd v Buckler*) turned on the technical effect of 1974 unilateral licence
> letters addressed to “Mrs Buckler” – a name my grandmother Mary Williams
> (née Williams) never used in her marriage or death records. By addressing
> her under this legal fiction, the proceedings bypassed any adjudication of
> the Williams equitable title that had been recognised as late as 1915. As
> the principle “fraud unravels all” makes clear, once the foundational
> misnomer is identified, the entire chain of subsequent possession orders,
> licences and registration falls to be re-examined. My grandmother and her
> heirs therefore retain the superior land claim; the 1988 dispossession and
> demolition of the 800-year-old farmhouse constitute actionable loss for

Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your e-mail and additional information explaining the background to your enquiry.

Unfortunately, apart from the pre-war survey returns The National Archives has only the only information recorded on-line MDR, and the following entry appears most pertinent to your enquiry held at the Glamorgan Archives: court book, with other manors D/D B M/3  for 1884-1937 held at Glamorgan Archives. We do not hold any other finding manorial finding aids such as old index cards as the entries were updated in 1990’s summarising the archive services catalogues of the time. Also, I have no more access or information relating to the various archive collections held outside of The National Archives than any other researcher. The Bute Estate Archives held at the Glamorgan Archive Service are catalogued under collection reference DB: Bute, Glamorgan Estate 

The only physical source we hold is a paper copy of the catalogue of 370 pages of the ‘Stuart family, Marquesses of Bute Archives: manorial records and estate papers, mainly rel to Glamorgan and Monmouthshire estates’ deposited at the National Library of Wales (NLW) in July 1950 (Ref. NRA 581) which submitted to the National of Register of Archives which now has a summarised entry in our on-line catalogue Discovery: Glamorganshire (Cardiff, Llantrisant, etc) and Monmouthshire (Newport, Machen, etc, NRA Stuart 581  The reference to the Manors of Leckwith, Llandough, Cogan Cosmeston and Walterson is M17, pages 113-116 of the catalogue although most of the material predates 1900. This can be viewed at the library reading room at The National Archive by prior appointment. The Bute Estate archives for Glamorgan appear to be held at the National Library of Wales and the Glamorgan Archive Service. The NLW paper catalogue (Ref. NRA 581) broadly mirrors the NLW on-line catalogue: Bute Estate Records, - National Library of Wales Archives and Manuscripts 

A possibility worth bearing in mind is that the property, Great House Farm / Ty Mawr / Cedfin may ceased to have been held by copyhold tenure by 1900 and instead may have been held instead by a leasehold tenancy which if this was the case the manorial records will not be relevant to your research. As you mentioned the Bute estate interests were steadily disposed of from c1900 culminating in sale of the estate’s leasehold interest to the Western Ground Rents Company in 1938. This led to the widespread dispersal and possibly destruction of the Bute estate records which makes it particularly challenging to track down and identify individual documents. Furthermore, catalogues often include bundle lists with individual documents concealed by a general description of the contents of the whole bundle.

I regret I cannot be of any further assistance; however I hope your further research proves fruitful.

Kind regards

Dear Mr. Gale,

Thank you again for your helpful reply and for viewing the original Manorial Documents Committee returns (HMC9/311). I entirely understand that it is difficult to advise further without more specifics, and I am grateful for the steer toward the Penrice and Margam Estate Records and the NLW catalogue.

To answer your question directly: the document historically referred to within the family as the “Williams Title” (or the equitable interest conveyance that underpinned it) dates to the period c. 1900–1915. It arises from an agreement between John Williams (occupier of Great House Farm / Ty Mawr / Cedfin) and Daniel Thomas & Son (Bute Estate quarry operators / limestoners). In essence, the Williams family granted permission for quarrying on part of the farm in return for equitable title / permanent security of tenure once quarrying was complete. Daniel Thomas is said to have formalised his side by a land-swap deed with the Bute Estate (copy formerly held in Cardiff Library, now reported missing along with its index card in 1984).

This places the key transaction squarely in the early 20th-century Bute estate rationalisation period, immediately before the 1916 agricultural tenancy to John Williams and the 1915 death of Daniel Thomas (after which Bute attempted eviction, only for the equitable interest to be asserted successfully at the time). Family testimony, supported by the 1876 limeworks severance (Glamorgan Archives D153/4-8) and the known industrial quarrying context, points to this narrow window as the origin of the modern title dispute.

Why this matters now The 1987 Court of Appeal decision (BP Properties Ltd v Buckler) turned on the technical effect of 1974 unilateral licence letters addressed to “Mrs Buckler” – a name my grandmother Mary Williams (née Williams) never used in her marriage or death records. By addressing her under this legal fiction, the proceedings bypassed any adjudication of the Williams equitable title that had been recognised as late as 1915. As the principle “fraud unravels all” makes clear, once the foundational misnomer is identified, the entire chain of subsequent possession orders, licences and registration falls to be re-examined. My grandmother and her heirs therefore retain the superior land claim; the 1988 dispossession and demolition of the 800-year-old farmhouse constitute actionable loss for which reparations are now sought.

To strengthen the evidential base I have prepared a one-page interactive timeline (hosted at [insert your hosted link here after uploading]) that highlights every event directly relevant to the “Williams Title” period. With your elevated archival access, you will immediately see where to focus searches in the Penrice and Margam or Bute collections (e.g., 1895–1916 leases, conveyances, limeworks/quarrying files, and any Daniel Thomas references).

I would be most grateful if you could now guide me to the precise sub-series or box references within those collections that cover Llandough manorial transactions in the 1900–1916 window. Any surviving index cards, rental entries, or correspondence mentioning John Williams / Daniel Thomas in connection with Great House Farm would be transformative.

Thank you once more for your time and expertise. I look forward to your further assistance.

Kind regards

Sion Buckler

*       Licence correspondence dated 31 October 1974 surfacing only on 4 November, potentially interrupting proceedings to prevent hearings.

*       Claims of 1974 benevolent withdrawal under press scrutiny unsupported by verifiable coverage.

*       Land registration before Mary Williams’s 1983 death without title determination; disputes possibly lodged/suppressed by Land Registry.

*       Inconsistent treatment of BP entities across proceedings to family detriment.

*       Procedural barriers preventing effective defense (e.g., interrupted essential services post-licence; 1960–1987 court rulings dismissing ancestral title as "notion" without evidence).

*       Knowing bypass of archaeological constraints (e.g., 1978 trenches ignored; no contemporaneous 1970s/1990s press on discoveries amid development).

*       Missing key documents (e.g., 1667 conveyance, 1811–1835 Lambert Williams agreements proving status, 1982–84 library deeds vanishing).

*       Risks of further erasure: Heritage databases celebrate "Llandough Roman villa cemetery" while omitting our saga; modern residents unaware of the "battleground" site.



These anomalies suggest systemic theft, from colonial English subjugation (e.g., 1543–1770 orbit shifts) to corporate siege, during Wales' cultural/economic transitions. Authority derived through such means is illegitimate under natural justice, customary Welsh principles, and moral-legal frameworks. The record's distortion secures advantage, but passage of time does not validate it.



Preliminary assessment indicates cumulative benefits from redevelopment (absent title extinguishment) exceed £100 million, forming a basis for reparations—covering lost land, artifacts, livelihood, and trauma.



I require relevant public servants, custodians, and office-holders (including Land Registry, heraldry bodies, museums, archaeologists, MPs, historians, and councillors) to cease delay, engage substantively, review/correct/annotate records where defective, and prevent further rewriting of history. Justice delayed is denied, especially with verifiable evidence available.



This Notice:



*       Challenges the record's accuracy, completeness, and legitimacy.

*       Place assertions of title/standing on record pending adjudication.

*       Reserves all rights without prejudice.

*       Puts officials/beneficiaries on notice that silence/reliance may aggravate responsibility.



For the avoidance of doubt, His Majesty the King was notified yesterday.



This serves as an invitation to engage constructively before reliance becomes untenable.



Regards, Sion Buckler On behalf of the Buckler–Williams family [address redacted], Dinas Powys, Vale of Glamorgan, Wales. https://bpvsbuckler.datro.xyz/  



Postscript — Disability and Succession (Material Notice): The heir-apparent to the asserted Manorial Lordship is Rhys Buckler’s son, a young man with Down syndrome. Any obstruction, marginalisation, or differential treatment affecting his inheritance would engage the Equality Act 2010 and UK international obligations on disability rights. Disability cannot bar succession or recognition. This is recorded to prevent claims of ignorance.
